To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of artificial neural networks to analyze pain data from patients with spinal cord stimulators provides additional information about technical outcome that is not obtained by standard statistical methods; (2) the use of the artificial neural networks provides a method of optimizing stimulation parameter and electrode placement for individual patients that is not available with standard statistical methods; and (3) the use of this method provides an objective, quantified, and statistically significant improvement in pain relief in patients with spinal cord stimulation.
the use of artificial neural networks in conjunction with a pain drawing methodology provides a new approach to optimizing spinal cord stimulator placement in patients with chronic pain.

(a) the neural network approach outperforms the linear discriminant analysis in the classification of the technical goal of spinal cord stimulation; and (b) the neural network method is able to identify a set of parameters that are associated with the technical goal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of a computerized pain drawing method for use in spinal cord stimulation and with the application of artificial neural networks to this problem.
the development of a computerized method of pain drawing that allows the patient to represent the overlap of pain and stimulation.
the development of new methods for the analysis of the structure and the dynamics of the brain and the application of these methods to the study of brain function in health and disease.
